programs: English BA, English MA, Creative Writing MFA, and Technical Communication MS, administered by the department, with the CRDM PhD and the Digital Humanities graduate certificate, in which English faculty teach. The BA's concentrations file one set of outcomes. Service courses (ENG 101, the ENG 33x sequence) have no program-level record, so their rows come from course outcomes

program_rows.reading: Documented on four of five outcomes, with the widest multimodal vocabulary among the undergraduate records in the set (language-based, visual, verbal, multimedia, and digital texts and works, audiences and purposes, rhetorical situation, form). Outcome 4, projects drawing on a range of cultural texts, names the product and its sources without the act. The record names what students make and interpret, where the degree's judgment sits inside those acts differs by concentration, which is where the mapping session begins.

Documented on three outcomes (present, write, edit). Seven of eighteen statements are departmental commitments about funding, recruiting, mentoring, and time to degree, which the codebook sets aside. One outcome names documentation as a genre without the act.

Silent in the record. Three learning outcomes name the thesis as a product (novel, collection), critical reading of fiction and poetry, and knowledge of the profession, and none names the act of writing as such. Five statements are faculty expectations.

Documented on ten of ten learning outcomes, several through the parent objective on professional development in technical communication. The program names genres and media (visual, verbal, multimedia, interactive), rhetorical situations and audiences, and, in outcome 2, what writing technologies do to the understanding of text, which is the AI question in the vocabulary the program already uses. Three statements are program commitments about recruiting and faculty.

Documented on six of ten learning outcomes, carried by the parent objective on professional success and by publication and presentation venues. Outcome 1d names ethical practices, including labor, as part of professional expectations. Five statements are program commitments (recruiting, placement, mentoring, progress to degree) and are not learning outcomes. CRDM is co-housed by English and Communication.

Documented on all seven learning outcomes, with the widest multimodal vocabulary in the graduate set (visual, multimodal, digital, media, design, scholarly communication in print and online). The remaining six statements are certificate satisfaction items. Included because English faculty teach in it and because, as an existing CHASS certificate with filed outcomes, it is the nearest template for the AI Learning Pathway certificate.

example.outcome: 1. Interpret a variety of language-based, visual, and digital texts for different audiences and purposes by applying appropriate critical frameworks.
example.site: Upper-division seminar in the concentration: interpretive essay (the working group names the course and the assignment)
example.act: Write an interpretation of a text applying a named critical framework, and adapt the argument to a stated audience
example.model: A model produces a competent interpretation under a named framework on request. As filed, the outcome gives a reader no way to separate the student's choice of framework and evidence from a generated one, and what the generated reading omits is the student's account of why this framework and this passage.
example.reason: Interpretation is the judgment the degree certifies. Students are permitted to use a model to test a reading against counter-readings. They choose the framework and the evidence, write the interpretation themselves, and state what the tool supplied and why they kept or rejected it.
example.revised: Students will interpret language-based, visual, and digital texts for stated audiences and purposes by applying critical frameworks they choose and defend, and will state the reasons for their decisions about any AI use in doing so.

literacy.describe: English studies the system's medium. A large language model produces text by predicting likely sequences from a corpus of prior writing, and the department's programs name the acts the model imitates: interpreting texts under a framework (BA, MA), making a work of original accomplishment (MFA), analyzing what writing technologies do to text, its invention, and its use (Technical Communication MS, outcome 2), and framing questions in a conceptual vocabulary (CRDM). Describing the system in the unit's terms means naming, program by program, which of these acts a model performs on the surface.
literacy.analyze: The structural questions belong to the field's own traditions: authorship and voice, the labor and the uncredited texts in a training corpus, whose language a model treats as standard, and what a generated reading or draft leaves out. The Technical Communication MS already states this analysis as an outcome. The CRDM PhD names ethical practice, including labor, in outcome 1d. Each program brings a different body of theory to the same question.
literacy.decide: The operative question differs by program, because a literary interpretation, a poem, a set of instructions for a user, and a dissertation chapter certify different judgments, so the department's decisions will differ by program and by assignment. For each outcome the Lab records the decision and its reason, counting refusal with a reason as a decision.

policy_intro: CWSP read the unit-level record in English and writing programs at NC State's twelve official peers, then the statements of the field's societies: MLA, CCCC, AWP for creative writing, the IEEE Professional Communication Society for technical communication, and AWAC for writing across the curriculum. For each document, the entry gives its scope and CWSP's reading of where its language breaks down, offered for the working group to correct.
policy_finding: Peer English departments have written statements of position and left rules to instructors. Rutgers English argues for critical AI literacy and leaves the decision to each instructor, the Georgia writing program declines a single policy, and Georgia Tech's writing program requires every instructor to hold one, chosen from four options. Across the same years the field moved from guidance to rights: the MLA-CCCC task force recommended policy set in tiers (institution, program, class) in 2024, and in March 2026 CCCC affirmed a right of students and teachers to refuse generative AI in the writing classroom. A program writing policy at NC State would decide at the level the 2024 guidance asks for while protecting the refusal the 2026 resolution affirms. Because each of the department's programs also answers to a different society, the MFA, the Technical Communication MS, and the literature and rhetoric programs face different disciplinary statements.

policies.governs: Classroom instruction, advice to the administration
policies.says: Sets no ban and no permission. Each instructor decides how AI is used against the course's learning goals. Calls generative AI the product of centuries of human labor, asks for critical AI literacies built with students, rejects detection tools as surveillance with faulty and discriminatory results, and asks the administration to consult faculty before buying or endorsing AI tools.
policies.glitch: Rutgers English argues at the level of the department and leaves the decision to the instructor, so the department's reasons reach a course only where an instructor carries them into a syllabus. Because the department dated nothing, readers have no way to tell which state of the tools the statement answers.

policies.doc: Requirements for Developing Generative AI Tool Policies in WCP Courses
policies.governs: Course policies for every WCP instructor
policies.says: Every instructor must have a policy. The recommended option allows AI in instances the instructor specifies. The others allow it broadly, bar it as an Honor Code matter, or let the instructor write a policy, each with the director's approval. Three principles bind students: responsibility, transparency, and documentation, with AI output cited as other sources are. Detectors are called unreliable and a ban hard to enforce.
policies.glitch: The program dated its understanding to July 2023 and promised development over 2023 and 2024, then cited a 2024 resource without changing the date. Since barring AI needs the director's approval and the recommended option does not, refusal becomes the choice a teacher has to justify.

policies.unit: First-year Writing Program, Department of English
policies.doc: FYW Guidebook, Chapter 7: Generative AI and First-Year Writing
policies.says: Has not designated a single, standardized AI policy, because instructor approaches vary. Students are expected to be the sole author of every submission, and even authorized uses require credit or citation. The university's default prohibits AI in coursework unless an instructor allows it.
policies.glitch: Sole authorship and authorized use sit side by side: a student permitted to use AI and required to credit it is no longer the sole author the same paragraph demands.

policies.unit: Coalition of Writing Across the Curriculum (includes the UA Writing Program)
policies.doc: Coalition of Writing Statement on AI Writing
policies.says: Treats writing as a mode of learning and advises redesigning assignments toward visual, recorded oral, and collaborative work. Holds a campus ban hard to enforce and likely to penalize students with communication disabilities or students who rely on grammar and tutoring tools.
policies.glitch: Although the Coalition wrote the statement in spring 2023 against one product, ChatGPT, the university still links it from its AI page as current guidance, the kind of temporal artifact the principle on dating a policy addresses.

policies.doc: Statement on Generative AI and Writing
policies.says: The authors (Jason Crider and Andrew Pilsch) describe a department statement meant to demystify generative AI and explore it within the teaching of writing. The department has since announced an AI writing lab funded by an alumna's gift. The statement itself was not retrieved in this run.
policies.glitch: Reading pending. Retrieve the statement and correct this entry before the session.

policies.inst: Purdue, Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Maryland, UC Davis, Virginia Tech, Michigan State, Minnesota
policies.says: Silent at the unit level. Each campus leaves AI policy to the instructor through syllabus guidance. Minnesota's first-year writing program, by its directors' account, expects every section to state its policy and discuss AI with students, without a common policy.
policies.glitch: The departments whose faculty write the field's scholarship on AI and writing have left the policy to the syllabus, where the reasons a program holds in common are written once per course.

policies.unit: MLA-CCCC Joint Task Force on Writing and AI
policies.says: Working Paper 1 sets principles and calls for critical AI literacy at every level. Working Paper 2 recommends policy set in tiers, institution, program or department, and class, so programs protect assessments requiring no AI while students build AI literacy. The task force ended in early 2025, succeeded by the MLA Task Force on AI in Research and Teaching.
policies.glitch: The task force wrote for a tiered system and presumed a program tier, which most peer departments in this run have not built.

policies.unit: Conference on College Composition and Communication
policies.says: Affirms the rights of students and teachers to refuse to sign up for, prompt, or otherwise use generative AI in the writing classroom, extending the 1974 Students' Right to Their Own Language. Asks for refusal to be accounted for in course design and assessment, against policing and punishing student use, for disclosure of AI in grading, and never to put student work into a model without consent.
policies.glitch: A right held by each teacher and each student sits uneasily with the program tier the 2024 working paper recommends, since a program requiring AI in an assignment would have to provide an alternative for any student who refuses.

policies.unit: Executive Council, drafted by the MLA Task Force on AI in Research and Teaching
policies.doc: Statement on Educational Technologies and AI Agents
policies.says: Addresses AI browser agents completing assignments inside learning management systems. Asks companies to reduce misuse, holds the burden of blocking agents should not fall to educators alone, and calls for faculty seats on the committees choosing educational technology.
policies.glitch: The Executive Council locates the problem with vendors and procurement, outside any program's control, while the department's assignments sit inside the platforms the statement names.

policies.unit: Association of Writers and Writing Programs
policies.governs: Teaching guidance for creative writing programs
policies.says: AWP issued recommendations with resources and guidelines for teachers in 2025, followed by panels on AI pedagogy and publishing. The document sits behind member access and was not read in this run.
policies.glitch: Because AWP keeps its guidance for MFA programs behind member access, an MFA program citing it gives students a reason they have no way to read.

policies.doc: Professional Guidance on Artificial Intelligence in Professional Communication
policies.governs: Professional practice and technical communication education
policies.says: Treats AI as part of technical information systems, asks programs to integrate AI literacy into communication design and education, and casts communicators as stewards of ethical technology use. ATTW has issued no statement.
policies.glitch: The working group disclosed using ChatGPT to draft and refine the guidance, a disclosure of the kind it asks of practitioners, made without saying which passages the tool shaped.
